item.title: [DEV Community: javascript] Best WebGL fluid simulations for motion studies
item.description:
This comparison is about interactive, pointer-driven fluid in the browser: you move the cursor or a finger, and ink-like or particle-driven motion responds in real time. That is a narrower job than a general Three.js scene, a decorative animated background with no fluid solver, or a desktop CFD package.

This article was written with the assistance of AI.

One fact belongs at the top. The WebGL fluid simulation page on Uwarp describes itself as powered by Pavel Dobryakov’s public WebGL fluid demo (“Pavel DoGreat”). It is a hosted entry to that well-known project, not a separately invented solver. The original demo is therefore included as the canonical source.

This is not a GPU benchmark and does not name an overall winner. Performance varies by device, as several of the pages themselves note.

The same checks apply: official demo and source URLs; what you can control; license if published; whether the page is an original project or a host; and any motion-accessibility caveats.

Pavel Dobryakov’s WebGL Fluid Simulation

The original project lives at GitHub: PavelDoGreat/WebGL-Fluid-Simulation, with a live demo at paveldogreat.github.io/WebGL-Fluid-Simulation. It is the widely cited GPU fluid demo that many later pages embed or fork. Use this URL when you want the author’s project, issue tracker, and source, or when you need to check the license in the repository rather than on a wrapper page.

Because it is a shader-heavy, full-viewport experience, it can be intense for motion-sensitive viewers. Offer a still or a reduced-motion alternative if you reuse the idea in a product UI.

Best fit: the canonical demo and source for this exact ink-trail fluid effect. Trade-off: it is a demo, not a drop-in design-system component; integrating it into production is your own engineering work.

GPU Fluid Experiments (George Corney / haxiomic)

GPU Fluid Experiments by George Corney is another official, interactive WebGL fluid demo, with source at github.com/haxiomic/GPU-Fluid-Experiments. It has also been listed among Google’s Experiments. It is a related but distinct project — a second mature GPU fluid experiment you can open in a tab and study — not a reskin of Dobryakov’s repo.

As with any WebGL fluid demo, performance depends on the machine, and the official pages should be checked for license terms before you ship a derivative.

Best fit: a second, independently authored GPU fluid experiment for comparison and study. Trade-off: different controls and look; not a drop-in replacement for the DoGreat demo if you were trying to match that exact aesthetic.

Vanta.js (related, but not the same solver)

Vanta.js is a popular library for animated website backgrounds (three.js / p5.js). It can produce atmospheric motion, but it is not documented as the same pointer-driven Navier–Stokes ink simulation as the DoGreat demo. It is included here only as a clearly labeled adjacent option: useful when you wanted a lighter hero background, not when you needed that specific fluid-solver behavior.

Best fit: decorative animated backgrounds in a site hero. Trade-off: do not treat it as a substitute fluid simulation; the task is different.

Hosted WebGL fluid demo

The WebGL fluid simulation on Uwarp is a browser page for pointer- or touch-driven ink-style trails. The product page attributes the effect to Pavel Dobryakov’s public build and describes GPU WebGL rendering, real-time response, and no-install viewing for motion studies, hero-background inspiration, and visual-showcase references. It also notes that performance can vary by GPU and refresh rate, and that motion-heavy visuals may need an alternative for reduced-motion needs.

For source, license, and upstream updates, the official GitHub project remains the authority. A wrapper page can lag behind the repo.

Best fit: a convenient hosted URL for the DoGreat-style demo when you want to share a link for a motion review. Trade-off: it is not an original solver; check the upstream project for license and the latest code.

Choose the original when you need the source

For this exact fluid effect, start with Dobryakov’s demo and repository. Use the Uwarp page as a hosted viewing URL if that is more convenient, but attribute the work correctly. Use Corney’s GPU Fluid Experiments when you want another serious WebGL fluid project to compare. Use Vanta only when you actually wanted a background library rather than a fluid solver.

If you embed any of these in a landing page, plan for reduced motion, battery, and low-power GPUs. A beautiful demo can still be a poor default for a documentation site.

item.title: [DEV Community: javascript] AbortError: signal is aborted without reason, and why my error tracker saw it
item.description:
AbortError: signal is aborted without reason is the message Chrome and Edge give the error an AbortController creates when you call controller.abort() with no argument. Firefox and Safari give the same error a different text: The operation was aborted. On my Social Downloader it came from a timeout of my own, which my code caught. It still reached error tracking as unhandled, because a second promise chained off the same fetch had no catch. Passing abort() a reason, and filtering on the error's name rather than its text, fixes both halves.

What does "signal is aborted without reason" mean?

abort() takes an optional reason. When you leave it out, the signal makes one for you: a DOMException named AbortError. Every fetch using that signal rejects with that exception.

const controller = new AbortController()
controller.abort()

console.log(controller.signal.reason.name)    // "AbortError"
console.log(controller.signal.reason.message) // Chrome: "signal is aborted without reason"
                                              // Firefox, Safari: "The operation was aborted."

The message means code in the page cancelled the request and gave no explanation. A network failure or a server refusal looks different (see the FAQ below).

Where mine came from: a timeout with no reason

The downloader resolves a TikTok link two ways at once. The browser asks a public API directly, and the server resolves the same link in parallel. Whichever answers first wins. The browser call has a 6 second budget, written like this (trimmed to its shape):

async function resolveInBrowser(url) {
  const controller = new AbortController()
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 6000)
  try {
    const response = await fetch(endpoint(url), { signal: controller.signal })
    if (!response.ok) return null
    return parse(await response.json())
  } catch {
    return null // timeout, offline, blocked: let the server answer
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer)
  }
}

The fetch and the .json() both sit inside the try, and the catch turns a timeout into null. On 27 November a visitor on Edge pasted a link to a TikTok photo post. The browser call ran out its 6 seconds, the server answered that it could not resolve the post, and the app showed that message, as designed. Four milliseconds later the error tracker recorded AbortError: signal is aborted without reason, marked as unhandled.

Why a caught AbortError can still show as unhandled

The event had one stack frame, in one of my own bundles. I fetched that bundle from production and read the code at the frame's column. It was the controller.abort() inside the timer, which says less than it seems to. A DOMException records its stack when it is created, and abort() creates it. So the frame shows who cancelled the request, not who failed to handle the rejection. Every promise that rejects with this exception carries the same stack, wherever it was left unhandled.

My promise was handled, so the unhandled one had to be someone else's. Any script that patches window.fetch to watch requests can make a second promise from the original:

const originalFetch = window.fetch
window.fetch = function (...args) {
  const request = originalFetch.apply(this, args)
  request.then((response) => record(response)) // a second promise, never caught
  return request
}

The page gets request back and catches it. The .then() the wrapper made is a separate promise, and it rejects with the same AbortError. Nothing catches that one, so the browser fires unhandledrejection, and an error tracker listening for it reports the cancel as a crash. Browser extensions, analytics snippets and ad scripts all patch fetch this way. The stack does not say which one it was, and I could not find out. I could check that every path in my code caught it, and it did.

How to tell if the error is yours

  1. Check how it was captured. An error tracker that marks it handled: false caught it from unhandledrejection or window.onerror, not from your own catch.
  2. Map the frame to code. Fetch the production bundle and read the code at the frame's line and column. If Cloudflare or a bot filter sits in front of the site, send a browser User-Agent, or you will get a challenge page instead of JavaScript.
  3. If the frame is an abort() call, read every promise that uses that signal. When each one is awaited inside a try, or has a .catch(), the unhandled copy is not yours.
  4. Read the session around it. Mine showed resolve_failed 4 ms before the exception: the cancel was the timeout doing its job.

How to fix it

Give abort() a reason, and the rejection says what happened in every browser:

setTimeout(() => controller.abort(new DOMException('tikwm timed out', 'TimeoutError')), 6000)

// or let the platform do it:
fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(6000) }) // rejects with a TimeoutError

If you switch to TimeoutError, check every catch that tests error.name === 'AbortError'. A timeout no longer matches it, so code that treats a cancel as "the user changed their mind" will now treat a timeout as a failure. That is usually what you want, but check it on purpose.

For the error tracker, filter on the name, or on every engine's text. My error filter already dropped this cancel, but only in Safari's wording, The operation was aborted. Chrome's wording went straight through. A pattern for one engine's message misses the others, so match them together:

const BARE_ABORT = /^(DOMException: )?AbortError: (The operation was aborted|signal is aborted without reason)\.?$/i

If your tracker gives you the exception type as a separate field, filter on AbortError there and skip the text entirely.

I also wrote about the same class of noise from injected scripts in __gCrWeb and __firefox__ errors: code that isn't yours, reported as if it were.

FAQ

Is "signal is aborted without reason" a network error?

No. The request was cancelled by code in the page calling abort(). A network failure shows up as TypeError: Failed to fetch in Chrome, not as an AbortError.

Why does Firefox say "The operation was aborted" instead?

The error is the same, a DOMException named AbortError. Each engine picks its own message text. Code that checks the name works everywhere, and code that checks the message works in one browser.

Should I report AbortError to my error tracker at all?

Not a bare one. A cancel you started is expected behaviour. If you need to know how often a timeout fires, count it as a product event with the reason attached, and keep the error board for things that are actually broken.

item.title: [DEV Community: javascript] What Changed in This npm Release? Compare the Tarballs Before Upgrading
item.description:
A dependency upgrade can change more than the function your application imports. It might add an install script, move a command-line entry point, or ship a directory that was absent from the previous release. The changelog gives you the author's explanation. Comparing the two published tarballs shows the changes your application will actually receive.

Start with the exact version in your lockfile and the exact proposed replacement. Avoid moving tags such as latest: the review should refer to the same pair of artifacts when a teammate repeats it tomorrow. Keep both archives until the upgrade decision is recorded.

Capture both releases in separate directories

You need npm and a Linux or WSL shell with tar, sort, diff, and sha512sum. Save the script below as compare-release.sh, then invoke it with two exact name@version arguments from the upgrade proposal. Use the same package name for both arguments. The script downloads archives and reads their contents without installing the packages.

npm pack accepts a package specification, can save the tarball to a chosen directory, and supports JSON output. The explicit --ignore-scripts flag suppresses lifecycle execution for this operation. That control does not establish that the package is safe to execute later; npm documents its scope in the ignore-scripts reference.

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
OLD=${1:?Pass the old exact name@version}
NEW=${2:?Pass the new exact name@version}
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir "$WORK/old" "$WORK/new"

npm pack "$OLD" --ignore-scripts --json \
  --pack-destination "$WORK/old" > "$WORK/old/pack.json"
npm pack "$NEW" --ignore-scripts --json \
  --pack-destination "$WORK/new" > "$WORK/new/pack.json"

for side in old new; do
  archive="$(find "$WORK/$side" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.tgz' -print -quit)"
  test -n "$archive"
  tar -tzf "$archive" > "$WORK/$side/files.unsorted"
  LC_ALL=C sort "$WORK/$side/files.unsorted" > "$WORK/$side/files.txt"
  tar -xOzf "$archive" package/package.json > "$WORK/$side/package.json"
  sha512sum "$archive" > "$WORK/$side/SHA512SUMS"
done

compare() {
  if diff -u "$1" "$2"; then
    :
  else
    status=$?
    [ "$status" -eq 1 ] || return "$status"
  fi
}
compare "$WORK/old/files.txt" "$WORK/new/files.txt"
compare "$WORK/old/package.json" "$WORK/new/package.json"
printf 'Review artifacts: %s\n' "$WORK"

The helper accepts diff exit status 1, which means differences were found, while preserving error statuses. The sorted lists make added and removed paths easier to see. They do not compare the contents of files whose names stayed the same. The manifest diff may also contain formatting changes, so read the field values before treating every changed line as a behavior change.

Read the manifest changes in execution order

First inspect lifecycle scripts. A new postinstall command deserves a specific question: what does it run, and why does this release need it? Follow the referenced file in the archive as text. A change from one script filename to another can matter even when the script's name in package.json remains unchanged.

Next inspect entry points. Changes to main, exports, or bin can redirect the code used by imports or command-line invocations. npm's package.json reference describes those fields along with dependency declarations. Compare dependencies, optionalDependencies, and peerDependencies separately: a new runtime dependency and a changed peer requirement create different upgrade work.

Check whether changed entry points refer to files that appear in the archive listing. A new executable path with a matching new file is a concrete review target. A missing target may instead indicate a packaging mistake that would break consumers.

Connect file changes to the release explanation

Suppose a hypothetical comparison shows these three changes:

Artifact difference Follow-up before approving
Added postinstall invoking scripts/setup.js Read the script and identify any subprocesses or downloads
bin now points to dist/cli.cjs Inspect the new entry point and check supported invocation behavior
Added vendor/ files Establish their purpose, origin, and relevance to the upgrade

These are review questions, not automatic rejection rules. A bundled native component may explain a new directory; removing unused sources may explain a much smaller archive. Unexplained changes should remain open items in the upgrade review.

For a manual exercise, compare one proposed upgrade against its currently locked version. Pick one changed manifest field and one changed file path. Trace each to the release notes or source change, and record whether the explanation accounts for what the archive contains. For a file present in both releases, inspect its contents too; identical filenames alone reveal nothing about changed behavior.

Attach the artifact identities to the decision

Keep the two exact package specifications, npm's pack output, archive checksums, and review notes together. The SHA-512 files identify the bytes inspected. Their hexadecimal output differs from the base64 encoding commonly used in integrity strings, so compare like encodings when checking against lockfile integrity metadata. A locally computed checksum alone establishes no publisher identity.

End the upgrade review with specific resolved questions: why the lifecycle command changed, where the new entry point leads, which dependencies were added, and what remains unexplained. That record gives the next reviewer a useful starting point if the package changes again.

item.title: [DEV Community: javascript] Build a local Notion MCP server with an explicit write allowlist
item.description:
A local MCP server can give Claude or Cursor two narrowly scoped Notion tools: read a page title and create a child page. The client launches Node and communicates with it over standard input and output. The server calls the hosted Notion API, and the MCP client receives the returned title or new page ID. Running the bridge locally does not make the workspace or the model session offline.

Choose the pages first

Create an internal Notion integration with read-content capabilities. Enable insert-content capabilities only if you intend to create pages. Share the relevant pages with the integration in Notion. Use a disposable parent for your first write. Format the 32-character page IDs as hyphenated UUIDs rather than pasting full URLs. The server applies two independent lists: permission to read a title never grants permission to write under that page.

Install and configure

Use Node 22 or newer. In an empty directory run:

npm init -y
npm install --save-exact @modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.2 zod@3.25.76

Supply NOTION_TOKEN through the local process environment using your existing secret manager. Set NOTION_READ_PAGES to a comma-separated list of page UUIDs. Leave NOTION_WRITE_PARENTS empty initially. A malformed ID stops startup. For clients launched from a desktop shortcut, verify that the launched server inherits these variables. Keep the token out of shared client configuration and source control.

Implement the server

Save the following as server.js in that directory. The parent ID is checked before the server builds the outbound POST. Callers can supply a title and parent ID only. They cannot choose the destination URL, integration token, or arbitrary page properties.

const { McpServer } = require("@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js");
const { StdioServerTransport } = require("@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js");
const { z } = require("zod");

const id = z.string().uuid().transform(value => value.toLowerCase());
const title = z.string().trim().min(1).max(200);
function allowedPages(variable) {
  const raw = process.env[variable];
  if (!raw || !raw.trim()) return new Set();
  return new Set(raw.split(",").map(value => id.parse(value.trim())));
}

async function main() {
  const reads = allowedPages("NOTION_READ_PAGES");
  const writes = allowedPages("NOTION_WRITE_PARENTS");
  const token = process.env.NOTION_TOKEN;
  if (!token) throw new Error("Set NOTION_TOKEN");
  const server = new McpServer({ name: "local-notion", version: "1.0.0" });

  async function notion(path, options = {}) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.notion.com/v1/" + path, {
      ...options,
      headers: {
        Authorization: "Bearer " + token,
        "Notion-Version": "2025-09-03",
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
      },
      redirect: "error",
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)
    });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Notion returned HTTP " + response.status);
    return response.json();
  }
  function result(text) {
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text }] };
  }
  server.registerTool("read_title", {
    description: "Read the title of an allowed page",
    inputSchema: { page_id: id }
  }, async ({ page_id }) => {
    if (!reads.has(page_id)) throw new Error("Page is outside the read allowlist");
    const page = await notion("pages/" + page_id);
    const property = Object.values(page.properties).find(p => p.type === "title");
    return result((property?.title || []).map(t => t.plain_text).join(""));
  });
  server.registerTool("create_child", {
    description: "Create one child page under an allowed parent",
    inputSchema: { parent_id: id, title }
  }, async ({ parent_id, title }) => {
    if (!writes.has(parent_id)) throw new Error("Parent is outside the write allowlist");
    const page = await notion("pages", {
      method: "POST",
      body: JSON.stringify({
        parent: { type: "page_id", page_id: parent_id },
        properties: { title: { type: "title", title: [{ type: "text", text: { content: title } }] } }
      })
    });
    return result(page.id);
  });
  await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
}
main().catch(error => {
  console.error(error.message);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Connect and exercise the boundary

Configure your MCP client's local stdio server entry with the absolute path to the Node executable as the command and the absolute path to server.js as its sole argument. Restart the server after changing its environment. Tool discovery should show read_title and create_child. Because it uses stdio transport, no HTTP listener or background daemon is required.

First call read_title with an ID from the read list. Then request create_child with that same ID while the write list is empty. Expect an allowlist error and no outbound write. To enable one write destination, put the disposable parent UUID in NOTION_WRITE_PARENTS, restart the server and request a child titled “MCP smoke test”. Check the returned ID against the child in Notion. Another parent must still be denied. A successful local allowlist check cannot override Notion's own page-sharing rules or integration capabilities.

Handle an uncertain write

If a create request times out, inspect the intended parent before retrying. Notion may have created the page before the response was lost. The server makes one request and has no idempotency ledger. A caller that needs automatic retries must reconcile the first attempt.

The example was tested with a real MCP client and server over stdio and a fixture in place of the Notion API. The checks covered tool discovery, allowed reads, malformed input, denied destinations, an empty write list and the exact outgoing parent and title for an allowed write. Live workspace writes and desktop-client setup were outside that test.

item.title: [DEV Community: javascript] URLSearchParams Encodes Forms, Not URLs: A Practical Percent-Encoding Guide
item.description:
Percent-encoding bugs rarely announce themselves as encoding bugs. They appear as a search query that arrives with plus signs, a redirect that loops, an OAuth callback that fails only for an internationalized value, or an API that receives %2520 where it expected one space.
The usual cause is using one encoder for every part of a URL. JavaScript exposes several related functions, but they answer different questions:
URLSearchParams serializes form data. 
encodeURIComponent encodes a URI component. 
encodeURI encodes a complete URI while preserving separators. 
new URL() parses and normalizes a URL. 
Those APIs overlap, but they are not interchangeable.
A space can be %20 or +
Start with the smallest example:
encodeURIComponent("a b");
// "a%20b"

new URLSearchParams({ q: "a b" }).toString();
// "q=a+b"
Both outputs are valid in their intended context. %20 represents a space byte in URI syntax. + represents a space in application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the format used by HTML form submissions and by URLSearchParams.
The ambiguity appears when a value is decoded by the wrong parser:
new URLSearchParams("q=a+b").get("q");
// "a b"

new URLSearchParams("q=a%2Bb").get("q");
// "a+b"

decodeURIComponent("a+b");
// "a+b"
URLSearchParams treats an unescaped + as a space. decodeURIComponent does not. If a + is part of the original value, it must be encoded as %2B before the value is placed in form-style data.
This is why “just decode the query string” is not a complete rule. The parser must match the producer.
encodeURIComponent is for components
encodeURIComponent is the better default for one path segment or one query value:
const value = "https://example.com/a b?x=1";
encodeURIComponent(value);
// "https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fa%20b%3Fx%3D1"
That output is correct if the entire value is data inside another parameter. It is wrong if the goal was to encode only the path portion of a URL while keeping https:// and the query delimiter readable:
encodeURI("https://example.com/a b?x=1");
// "https://example.com/a%20b?x=1"
encodeURI preserves characters that have structural meaning in a complete URI, including :, /, ?, #, &, and =. That makes it useful for readable examples, but it is not a general-purpose query-value encoder.
The practical rule is:
Input
Suitable encoder
One query parameter value
URLSearchParams, or a strict component encoder
One path segment
encodeURIComponent plus a policy check for !'()*
A complete URL
new URL() for structure; do not encode the whole string
An HTML form submission
URLSearchParams / application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Binary data
Use bytes and the correct transport encoding, not URL encoding
Unicode is encoded as UTF-8 bytes
Percent-encoding operates on bytes. JavaScript strings contain UTF-16 code units, so the runtime must convert them to UTF-8 first.
encodeURIComponent("你好");
// "%E4%BD%A0%E5%A5%BD"

decodeURIComponent("%E4%BD%A0%E5%A5%BD");
// "你好"
Each Chinese character becomes three UTF-8 bytes:
你 -> E4 BD A0
好 -> E5 A5 BD
An emoji can require four UTF-8 bytes and therefore a longer percent sequence. The visible character count is not the encoded byte count.
This matters when building signatures, OAuth URLs, redirect URIs, webhook parameters, or request caches. Two strings that look equivalent in JavaScript can produce different bytes if one has undergone normalization. For identifiers and security-sensitive values, compare the exact encoded form required by the receiving system instead of relying on visual similarity.
Encode once, at the boundary
Double encoding happens when an already encoded value is passed through the same encoder again:
const once = encodeURIComponent("a b");
const twice = encodeURIComponent(once);

once; // "a%20b"
twice; // "a%2520b"
The second operation did not corrupt the string. It correctly encoded the % character in the first result. The bug is architectural: the value crossed an encoding boundary twice.
Keep a simple state model:
Keep application values decoded. 
Encode when constructing the query string. 
Decode once when parsing it. 
Do not re-encode a value that is already in transport form unless the protocol explicitly says so. 
Logging helps separate the states. Record the decoded value and the final URL, but never assume that a readable browser address bar means the server received the same representation.
Path and query encoding are different jobs
A URL is not one opaque value. It has components with different delimiters:
https://example.com/users/Alice Smith?q=a+b&sort=created#profile
The valid construction is component-aware:
const url = new URL("https://example.com/");
url.pathname = /users/${encodeURIComponent("Alice Smith")};
url.searchParams.set("q", "a+b");
url.searchParams.set("sort", "created");
url.hash = "profile";

console.log(url.href);
// https://example.com/users/Alice%20Smith?q=a%2Bb&sort=created#profile
Note that the original + inside the query value became %2B. Otherwise the next URLSearchParams parser would read it as a space.
new URL() validates structure
Use the URL parser before applying string substitutions:
try {
const u = new URL(input);
console.log({
protocol: u.protocol,
hostname: u.hostname,
pathname: u.pathname,
query: Object.fromEntries(u.searchParams),
});
} catch {
console.error("Invalid absolute URL");
}
This catches missing schemes, malformed IPv6 hosts, bad ports, and other structural failures that string concatenation obscures. It also exposes parsed query values through the form-style decoder, which is useful when that is the protocol in use.
For a relative URL, provide a base explicitly:
new URL("../guide?lang=en", "https://www.example.com/docs/start/");
Do not assume that a browser will preserve every input byte. Host normalization, default-port removal, path normalization, and query serialization can all change the final URL.
A verification pass that catches real failures
Before sending a constructed URL:
Round-trip ASCII, Unicode, emoji, spaces, +, %, &, =, ?, /, and #. 
Assert whether spaces are expected as %20 or +. 
Confirm whether the receiver expects one or several query values with the same key. 
Decode once and compare the resulting value with the original application value. 
Reject malformed % sequences instead of silently replacing them. 
Inspect the final absolute URL after new URL() normalization. 
Never log credentials, access tokens, API keys, or sensitive query parameters. 
The JsonMind URL encoder and decoder can reproduce the %20, +, Unicode, and malformed-input cases in the browser. The URL parser is useful for checking host, path, query, and fragment boundaries separately.
Percent-encoding is not one operation. It is a family of transformations tied to a specific URL component and protocol. Once those boundaries are explicit, most “URL encoding is broken” reports become short, reproducible test cases.
The author maintains JsonMind. The examples were checked with Node.js 24.17.0 and the WHATWG URL implementation it provides.

item.title: [JavaScript on Medium] I used to waste a ton of time messing with how a page looked, not realizing the real problem was…

item.title: [Svelte blog] Celebrating ten years of Svelte
item.description:
It started with a commit — specifically, this one. Ten years later, we’re far from done; software never is. But we’ve come an awful long way. Last week the community gathered in Ljubljana, at the third in-person Svelte Summit, to mark the anniversary.

To be completely honest, I expected the atmosphere to be a little subdued. Being enthusiastic about front end frameworks feels somewhat passé in the era of agentic coding and software factories, so a conference dedicated to one of the more boutique ones could easily have felt like a bit of a throwback.

But I was wrong. The energy was fantastic. We had two days of lively conversation and unbelievable demos in one of Europe’s most beautiful cities, with a slew of announcements that we’ll follow up on in more detail soon:

  • Custom renderers are now supported behind an experimental flag, allowing you to use Svelte to build native apps and terminal UIs and PDFs and just about anything else you can imagine.
  • Async Svelte is making real progress towards production readiness.
  • vite-devtools-svelte, which integrates with Vite DevTools, was moved into the Svelte organisation and is working towards a 1.0 release.
  • rsvelte, by Svelte core team member Yuichiro Yamashita, is a unified Svelte toolchain written in Rust. It’s not quite production-ready yet, but it is hilariously faster than the JavaScript equivalents.
  • Svelte is now a core framework for Storybook.
  • mdsvex, a markdown toolkit for Svelte components, reached version 1.0.

Naturally, we spent a lot of time talking about AI. Many of the announcements are directly relevant to agentic development (the devtools expose an MCP server, rsvelte makes it practical for fleets of agents to work on large apps concurrently, and so on), and most attendees described themselves as frequent — if ambivalent — users of the technology. But there’s nothing like an in-person gathering to remind you that the best bits of the job can’t be automated away.

Keep an eye on the Svelte Society YouTube channel, where the talks will be published in the coming days, starting with Unfinished business by yours truly.

We’re a decade in, and our best years are still ahead of us.

item.title: [JavaScript Weekly] Bundler-free npm imports in the browser
item.description:
#​812 — November 24, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

Nudeps: Bundler-Like Imports, None of the Baggage — What if you could npm install a package and import it by name in the browser without a bundler? Lea and Dmitry Sharabin's new tool makes this easier than ever using import maps (which it keeps up to date). Run npx nudeps install and add the import map script to your HTML. There are also demos to try.

Lea Verou

💡 This work follows on from Lea's popular essay earlier this year: Web Dependencies are Broken. Can We Fix Them?

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous shows the exhaustive impact of every PR, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

jQuery 4.1 Released (Plus a Goodbye to 3.x) — Most of us probably don't need it (just 16% of State of JS 2025 respondents use jQuery regularly) but it lives on in ~63% of sites, so if that includes yours, both releases fix a selector bug (that can hang the page) and 3.8 is 3.x's last planned feature release.

Timmy Willison (jQuery)

IN BRIEF:

  • Chrome 157/158's DevTools can now debug with original variable and function names (see above), including in minified code, if the source maps include data from the scopes proposal.

  • TC39 meets again next week (remotely this time). The agenda has text imports up for stage 4, immutable ArrayBuffers for stage 3, and AbortController-based cancellation for stage 2.

  • Ladybird, a 'truly independent' browser built from scratch (including its JS engine), is now in alpha. Simon Willison takes it for a spin here.

RELEASES:

  • webpack 5.113 – Building on its new built-in HTML and CSS support, webpack now scopes classes in <style module> blocks and updates matching names in the HTML.

  • 🔒 Bun 1.4.5 – A security release with fixes across HTTP/3, TLS, DNS and Zstandard, affecting Bun.serve, fetch, and several node: modules.

  • 🖼️ Jimp 2.0 – Image processing in pure JavaScript. A huge release that now also supports animated GIFs.

  • Nuxt 4.7, DOMPurify 3.5, Redux Toolkit 2.15, NestJS 12.6, vlt 1.8.1

📖  Articles and Videos

What Runs Your JavaScript? Engines vs Runtimes — Defining where a language ends and its supporting runtime begins can be tricky, especially for JavaScript with its unusual history and genesis in the browser. Mara explains the key moving parts, the difference between a host runtime and JavaScript itself, and how different JS implementations draw the line in various places.

Mara Averick

💡 The JavaScript engines zoo is worth a visit in its own right. It's a data table covering 139 JavaScript engines, their compliance, language they're built in, etc.

Foxit Compares 10 eSignature APIs — Embedded signing, webhooks, sandbox access, pricing and compliance, in one table you can shortlist from.

Foxit sponsor

Why I Switched to Vite+ — Is the unified Vite+ toolchain worth adopting? Ben, of the Vue core team, shares his impressions of how it works on his 97,000 line project and concludes it's worth the effort.

Ben Hong

Custom Renderers: Svelte Can Now Go Beyond the DOM — Svelte components can now render to WebGL, native UIs, or the terminal, say, with a 'custom renderer' telling Svelte how to create/update nodes there. It's experimental in Svelte 5.59 which just landed.

Paolo Ricciuti and the Svelte Team

💡 As an example of what this opens up, gpuix-svelte renders Svelte as a native desktop app using the Zed editor's GPUI. Yet another JS desktop/GUI app option!

Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit for Canvas — Safari famously caps page updates to 60 FPS by default, even on iPhones that go higher. But Rida found a sneaky way to get canvas rendering and touch input up to 120…

Rida F'kih

📄 To Remove Moment.js, We First Made Everything Depend on It – Replacing ~1000 date-handling call sites without changing what users see across locales. Medhat Dawoud

📄 Chrome Prerendering is Weird – It can run your site's JavaScript before you've even hit Enter in the address bar. Tom Bennet

📄 What's New in Angular 22.3? Cédric Exbrayat

🛠 Code & Tools

Component Party: See What Changes in Solid 2 — The long-standing 'Rosetta Stone' of UI frameworks (well worth revisiting in its own right) now covers Solid 2, and you can see a 'before and after' of numerous code examples in 2 vs 1.

Mathieu Schimmerling

Solid 2.0: The Long Hold — Five years after 1.0, the signals-based UI framework is now stable with async built right into its reactivity graph (so return a promise from a computation and everything downstream just handles it). Ryan explains the thinking, and why the SolidStart metaframework has been retired.

Ryan Carniato

💡 Ryan expands on the latter point in The Metaframework is Dead. Long Live the Metaframework, a 20-minute ViteConf talk.

Build Durable AI Agents & Workflows in TypeScript — Open-source and fault-tolerant. Tasks pick up right where they left off, even through failures, restarts, or deploys.

Trigger.dev sponsor

vlt Opens Its npm Package Mirror to Everyone — Clean installs can spend a lot of time downloading package metadata, but vlt's registry serves much less of it giving installs that can take 20-70% less time. No account/token is needed anymore, so give it a spin and see if it suits your setup.

Erick Wendel (vlt)

Astrobook: A Minimal Storybook Alternative — An alternative to the popular UI component playground that supports React, Vue, Preact, Svelte, Solid, Lit, and Astro. The demo site includes multiple framework examples.

Ocavue

  • 🕹️ melonJS 20.17 – Popular 2D game engine. Isometric and hexagonal Tiled maps are now drawn by the GPU.

  • Replay Node 26 – A 'time-travel' build of Node.js (for Linux x86-64 only) that records a run so you can debug it after the fact.

  • 📈 Frappe Charts 2.3 – Simple, zero-dependency SVG charts. Adds axis titles.

  • 🎵 OpenSheetMusicDisplay 3.0 – A way to render MusicXML sheet music.

  • jest-dom 8.0 – Custom DOM matchers for Jest and Vitest (5+ only).

  • Svelte Flow 2 – Node-based UI library.

📰 Classifieds

📸 Ditch the native app: Add QR, Data Matrix and EAN scanning to your web app with STRICH. Free 14-day trial, cancel anytime.

🚀 SpreadJS v20 is coming! Preview the major release of the industry-leading JavaScript spreadsheet at our Dec. 3 PM Office Hours livestream.

🎬 Reviewing AI PRs? TWD adds a video of each new test to the PR, so you see the UI change without checking out the branch. Free and MIT.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • React Anatomy (above) is a DevTools extension that splits a running React page into 3D layers showing its components along with live props. There's a demo you can try before installing anything.

  • 🔒 Hijacked GitHub accounts are being used to exploit servers that aren't patched against a variety of React and Next.js flaws and publish stolen credentials publicly. Here's some of what to check.

  • 🗳️ The State of JavaScript 2026 survey closes soon, so take it if you can. Browser developers pay attention to the results, so it's worth doing (plus the way they structure the survey means you can learn about various JavaScript features along the way).

  • 📊 Speaking of surveys, Devographics has also just published the State of HTML 2026 results. Kilian Valkhof sums them up here.

Deno and Astro joined Cloudflare. Nuxt and Svelte belong to Vercel. Tailwind and Remix joined Shopify. Anthropic acquired Bun, and OpenAI got the people from Pierre Computer Company (I'm just calling them out because they do very cool stuff).

And then there's Geoff. Geoff as in Geoff Graham, the editor of CSS-Tricks. After DigitalOcean bought the site that we all visited daily from Chris Coyier, it looked like another project was going to die because DigitalOcean seemed to have lost interest in it.

Not with Geoff, though, because he bought back CSS-Tricks from DigitalOcean. I have no idea about the deal size, but, oh boy, I definitely didn't see this one coming. And, of course, Geoff has big plans!

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

Many people shared that this feels like a long-awaited win for us, the bloggers, the educators. And I must admit I also felt a bit of encouragement after hearing the news. Maybe there's still a place for blogging, sharing, and learning together.

So, thank you, Geoff, for pushing forward. I really, really, really hope that this works out for you. And selfishly for us! ❤️

Something that made me smile this week

I don't know when or how I discovered Robert's blog. It feels very... wholesome? Browsing around gave me some good old blogging vibes. Robert also runs monthly themes, and this month's theme is "knowember".

If you're curious, here's my quick Knowember post.

Participate

No code

  • becoming yourself is a social project → "Most of us are surrounded by more care, intelligence, and help than we know how to access. Maybe part of reaching your potential is learning how to become easier to help."

A nice abstraction

That's a nice quick tip. Lean described how to turn document.currentScript into an inline templating engine. Love it!

Replace it!

For the image nerds: JPEG XL vs AVIF

You might have heard that JPEG XL is now supported by all major browsers. Should you use it? Jake put out a massive article comparing the new format with AVIF. Be warned, the article is very long, but the tl;dr at the top has you covered.

Choose wisely

Should buttons have cursor: pointer?

So, do you use cursor: pointer for buttons? I'm strongly in favor of doing this, but as it turns out, some people have strong opinions on the matter.

Decide

Rebuilding flex-wrap: balance

flex-wrap: balance; is so far only shipping in Chromium. If you still want to achieve balanced flex layouts, Ahmad shared some ways to come up with similar results.

Be balanced

The wonderful weird web – The nicest place

If today's one of those days when you could use a hug, you'll find one at the nicest place on the internet. Love the old-school vibes of the site.

Get a hug

Upcoming: headingoffset

Granted, it's not prime time yet for headingoffset (shipping in Firefox 162 first) and :heading(), but adjusting heading levels is a feature we've needed since the failed outline algorithm. Let's see when the other browsers pick this up!

Control your headings

The Navigation API

The Navigation API has been available in all browsers since January. Do you use it?

If not, Ollie went on a tour to describe what you can do with it. The posts are quick reads and give you a good idea of what's possible. Thank you, Ollie!

  • The navigate event
  • Initiating navigations with the Navigation API
  • Focus Management with the Navigation API
  • Preventing same-document and cross-document navigation

.PropFLIP

If you've been in the game long enough, you might remember the FLIP technique. FLIP allows you to use CSS transitions for animations that you would usually need JavaScript for. Now, the technique is from 2015, so there must be a more modern version, right?

That's what Adam was after, and he describes a modern approach to FLIP using @property.

Flip it!

Move all these grid items

And speaking of moving things around, did you know that you can use and transition anchor-positioned grid items? That's some fancy stuff!

Move them

A fancy range slider

As usual, I've no idea how Temani does it, but what you see above is a CSS-only input of type range, an output element, and a label. I've got no words!

Pick a value

Safari's new adaptive dark mode

If you're a Safari user and are bothered by bright websites, Safari 27.3 beta introduced a new feature to automatically turn bright websites dark. The feature respects color-scheme so that it doesn't clash with your dark mode styles, and if you want to disable the feature entirely, <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> is your friend.

Go dark

And apparently, Chrome ships an auto dark mode feature behind chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark, too. I wonder how many bug reports come in when browsers change how sites look natively.

No AI Slop: A Manifesto

Nothing more to add here than some quotes from the manifesto.

Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.

When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.

Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.

Don't be a slop cannon

Random MDN – :state()

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

I gotta be honest here: I hadn't seen :state() before. Dave explained how he uses "pseudo-pseudo-classes" to build interactive component demos and well... today I learned :state() is a web component thing.

The developers who thrive in this era will not be the ones with the highest output. They will be the ones whose output other people are glad to receive. Everyone else is generating work and calling it productivity.

item.title: [Release notes from remix] test v1.2.0
item.description:
Minor Changes

  • t.useFakeTimers() now fakes Date, performance.now(), setImmediate()/clearImmediate(), and AbortSignal.timeout() along with the timer functions, so wall-clock code such as expiry checks and timestamps can be tested without injecting a clock. While fake timers are active, Date.now(), new Date(), and performance.now() read the fake clock and move forward only with advance() or advanceAsync(). new Date(value), Date.parse(), Date.UTC(), and instanceof Date keep working. Immediates fire on the next advance(), and AbortSignal.timeout(ms) signals abort with a TimeoutError once the fake clock reaches ms. (#12203)

    Like Node's mock timers, the fake Date starts at the Unix epoch (0) and performance.now() starts at 0. Tests that used fake timers while reading the real Date, or while relying on real immediates or AbortSignal.timeout(), now see fake time instead. Pass the new now option to start at a specific time:

    let timers = t.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date('2030-01-01T00:00:00Z') })

  • Added data-property mocking with mock.property() and t.mock.property(), including read/write records, one-access value overrides, and descriptor restoration. Added getter and setter spies through mock.getter(), mock.setter(), and the fourth mock.method() argument. Exported MockTracker as the shared type for standalone and test-context mocks. (#12225)

    Test-context accessor and property mocks restore in reverse installation order after cleanup callbacks, even when a test or cleanup callback fails. Method mocks layered over getter spies preserve the accessor's backing value. Method, accessor, and property mocks can be created while Array.isArray is mocked, with array argument checks preserved.

  • Added public TestFn and TestMeta types for reusable test callbacks and metadata, with linked API documentation for the test body and its options. (#12226)

  • Add new t.waitFor(condition, { interval, timeout }) API to retry assertions until they pass. Polling stops when the test ends. See Polling Assertions for usage. (#12224)

Patch Changes

  • Fix several gaps in t.useFakeTimers(): (#12203)

    • clearTimeout() and clearInterval() now cancel real timers created before fake timers were enabled. Previously the fakes ignored those timers, so a test with a timeout option that enabled fake timers left its real timeout timer running after it finished, which later aborted the test's signal and kept the process alive.
    • setTimeout() and setInterval() now pass extra arguments to the callback.
    • In Node, fake timers return handles with ref(), unref(), hasRef(), and refresh(), so code that calls .unref() on a timer no longer throws. Clearing an expired timeout's handle prevents refresh() from reactivating it.
    • Calling t.useFakeTimers() again restores the previous clock before starting a new one, so cleanup restores the original Date. Repeated restore() calls have no effect.
    • Restore fake timers synchronously on abort and before user cleanup callbacks. Finished or aborted contexts cannot enable another clock, and runner deadlines keep using real timers.
    • Reject overlapping clocks, roll back failed installations, and restore the original property descriptors without reinstalling fakes beneath spies. Restoration attempts every property, reports failures, and permits retrying failed properties.
    • Keep fake timer IDs unique across clocks so clearing a stale numeric handle cannot cancel a later test's timer.
    • Fake AbortSignal.timeout(ms) validates its argument synchronously using Node's numeric integer range of 0 through 4294967295 in every runtime.

  • Fix test and lifecycle hook timeouts stalling under fake timers and prevent late timeouts from aborting completed test signals. (#12224)

item.title: [JavaScript Weekly] The top 10 things AI gets wrong in web development
item.description:
#​811 — November 17, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

npkill 1.0: Not Just for node_modules Anymore — npx npkill has long offered a way to find and remove waste from node_modules folders. Its first release in two years now also hunts down caches and build outputs like .next and .turbo, with 'profiles' for 20 ecosystems. If you're new to the tool, its homepage provides a good introduction.

Juan Torres

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous shows the exhaustive impact of every PR, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

UI SDK: Headless UI Behaviors for React, Vue, Svelte, & Solid — A new library from shadcn and Vercel that provides 50+ accessible, low-level behaviors, like roving focus, typeahead, popups, and drag and drop, that you compose into components (for several frameworks, plus Web Components).

Vercel

💡 𝕏 As shadcn says: "You and I don't need the same interfaces. We need the same interface behaviors." The idea is an agent, say, can generate whatever UI suits a task, with reusable focus, keyboard, and accessibility behaviors built in.

IN BRIEF:

  • Solid 2.0 is now stable, with 2.0.0 now on npm and the docs updated to match. There's no official announcement post (beyond the earlier Solid 2.0 RC posts) so expect more on this soon.

  • The Chrome team has proposed a Cross-Origin Storage API for sites to share large assets like AI models and WASM modules, so users would only have to download them once.

  • The cloud-based JavaScript hosting service Val Town is winding down with services ending January 10 and the code being open sourced in February.

  • The Bun team has published a dense technical tour of how its in-development ahead-of-time compiler works.

RELEASES:

  • Prettier 3.10 – The code formatter now supports the latest JavaScript proposals and new Flow syntax, and adds an opt-in plugin that swaps in the Zig-based Yuku's JS/TS parsers for speed.

  • 🎨 p5.js 2.4 – The creative coding library expands its SVG and 3D model support. Here's a starter sketch if you want to play quickly.

  • 🔒 Node.js v26.13.1 (LTS), v24.22.3 and v22.23.5 – The security releases we mentioned last week fix an HTTP/2 flaw that lets clients crash a server and an HTTPS bug that can leak other connections' memory.

  • PixiJS 3D – The popular 2D rendering library's official 3D engine is now in open beta. It's WebGPU-first, with a WebGL 2 fallback.

📖  Articles and Videos

📊 e18e's Ongoing Benchmarks of JavaScript Meta-Frameworks — The e18e performance initiative tracks releases of frameworks across the ecosystem (e.g. Nuxt, Astro, SvelteKit, SolidStart, and more), measuring everything from install size and build times to rendering speed. This dashboard is the place to dive in.

e18e

🤖 The Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development — The Chrome team examines where coding agents fall back on dated techniques, like hand-rolled focus traps instead of inert and JS overlays instead of popover, alongside gaps in passkey implementations and XSS defenses. A handy checklist for humans too.

Philip Walton (Google)

AI Security for Modern JavaScript & TypeScript — Traditional tools miss logic gaps. SonarQube Hunter Agent catches broken access control in your JS/TS CI/CD pipeline.

SonarSource sponsor

How a Third-Party Script Turned Malicious on Major Sites — An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely's A/B testing platform to inject a (now removed) malicious script into pages served to end users. Scott's analysis found it on sites including Zoom, the BBC, and GitLab, and shows how CSP can, and did, help.

Scott Helme (Report URI)

💡 Third-party scripts are an increasingly common attack vector, as Polymarket's users recently found. If you load any, brush up on CSP and Subresource Integrity, and if you provide them, see how Fathom secures theirs.

How Promises Really Resolve, Explained via a WebKit Bug — A contrived promise that should have thrown instead caused Bun and Safari (both of which use JavaScriptCore) to hang. Alistair fixed the bug and uses it to explain what resolve() actually does and why resolved isn't 'a real promise state'.

Alistair Smith

The Web Is More Than Enough — A reminder of how the vast array of powerful web platform APIs enables the development of complex apps in the browser, particularly as AI reduces the headaches involved in tying them together.

Paul Ford

Your JS Error Is Lying to You — Why can JSON.stringify(err) unexpectedly leave you with {}? Gabor presents a tour of what an Error holds, and how much of that makes it through stack traces, cause chains, worker boundaries, and loggers like Pino and Winston.

Gabor Koos

📄 How 13,000 Local Variables in a Function Overflowed V8's Stack – And why would that ever happen? It was the output of an OCaml to JS transpiler… :-) Jérôme Vouillon

📄 A Universal XSS in uBlock Origin via Its Element Picker – Leans on an interesting (and now fixed) postMessage and iframe exploit chain. Smitty van Bodegom

📄 Migrating 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in Three Weeks Daniele Rossino

🛠 Code & Tools

BrowserPod 4.0: A Linux-Like MicroVM for the Browser — A WASM-powered sandbox that runs Node, npm, git, and bash in the browser. Previously a metered service, v4.0 is free for any use, though it's not open source, and you must load it via their CDN (but no account or API key is needed).

Leaning Technologies

💡 Going somewhat deeper, Nitro creator Pooya Parsa has compiled the actual Linux kernel to WebAssembly (repo). It boots to a shell in under a second in modern browsers, or via npx unkernel (tip: use halt to exit!).

Debug Errors and Agents Faster: Sentry Changelog Live — A walkthrough of what’s new in debugging, from fixing prod bugs with Seer to tracing your agents. Register today.

Sentry sponsor

Kitesurf: Cloudflare's Browser Engine Now Open Source — An experimental browser for agents we featured in August. Mostly written in TypeScript and runs JavaScript in V8 isolates on Workers, with Rust compiled to WASM for layout and painting. There's no Chromium, and Puppeteer can drive it.

Cloudflare

File Viewer: A Multi-Format File Viewer for Internal Apps — Read-only views for Office, PDF/OFD, CAD, archives, email and other complex formats, with integrations for React, Vue, and Svelte. The docs site has demos showing off the formats covered.

Flyfish Dev

Flashwright: A Faster, API-Compatible Playwright Fork — Keeps Playwright's API and test runner, but reuses a browser context per worker and doesn't wait for animations to settle, plus similar tricks. Benchmarks show a ~2-4x speedup, while this post explains how it works.

Codebeast

React Flow 13: The Node-Based UI Library Gets Faster — The first major release in two years cuts re-renders in large flows, with new useNode and useEdge hooks. Vue Flow has joined the xyflow family too.

xyflow

  • SlickGrid 6.0 (above) – Long-standing data grid component. Now with zero dependencies, plus pinning on all four sides and sticky rows and columns. Examples and introductions on the project homepage.

  • XState v6 Beta – First beta of the state machine/actor library's next major version. The core API is considered stable and you can try it with xstate@beta.

  • 🕹️ Excalibur 1.0 – After 13 years, the 2D TypeScript game engine reaches v1 with 2D lighting, a plugin API, and a rebuilt Web Audio mixer. Sample games here.

  • 🕹️ JSNES 3.0 – JavaScript NES emulator. Now has a cycle-accurate core that passes all 134 'AccuracyCoin' tests. There are playable demos here.

  • type-fest 6.0 – Popular collection of essential TypeScript types (listed here). v6.0 adds 120 new types and requires TypeScript 6.

  • Fontkit 3.0 – Advanced font engine for Node and the browser. Now ESM-only, with a new core export so you can ship only the formats needed.

  • dts-bundle-generator 10.0 – A tool to tree-shake and bundle a project's TypeScript declarations into one file.

📰 Classifieds

📄 Parsing PDFs for a RAG or invoice pipeline? Foxit compares 10 document parsing APIs on output format, billing units and accuracy claims.

🌙 Agents can test mobile code at 3am. Expo Simulators gives them cloud simulators, so the loop runs while you sleep.

Stop being the middle manager for your coding agents. CodeAF runs the org, and only what no manager can settle reaches you. #1 on DeepSWE.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • You Don't Need jQuery, the long-standing guide to replacing jQuery methods with plain JavaScript, has had a big v3.0 update. Internet Explorer fallbacks are out in favor of modern one-liners like el.replaceChildren(), structuredClone(), and Promise.withResolvers().

  • Adam Argyle shares PropFLIP, a take on FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) animations where four @property custom properties do the inverting and a CSS transition does the playing.

  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, an official local emulator you can point your AWS SDK or CLI at, covering hundreds of its service interfaces. It's largely aimed at agents, and was built with them too.

  • 🎂 Happy birthday to Svelte! Svelte turned ten years old on Monday (Rich Harris made its first commit on November 16, 2016).

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

How X (Twitter) is Rebuilding Its Web App — X is replacing 3 servers with one app built on React, Vite and Fastify. It runs as a standalone binary without Node, with support for native plugins written in Rust, Go or Swift, while JavaScript plugins run on an embedded QuickJS runtime.

The Parcel Team

  • TypeScript 7's Go-powered compiler now has an experimental WebAssembly build which already powers an early TypeScript Playground v2.

#​809 — November 3, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

The AI Cost of JavaScript Frameworks

Nolan Lawson had Claude build the same app five times in each of twelve JS stacks to test common "X is better for agents" claims. Costs varied significantly between runs, and Gautam Parab found that the observed cost ranges overlapped or touched for most pairs of frameworks.

But a clearer difference was in the median amount of JavaScript sent to browsers: 0KB for Astro, 18K for Hono+htmx, 36K for SvelteKit, and 115–142K for React Router, TanStack Start and Next.js. If you've gone "hands-free", Nolan asks, why stick to a particular stack you chose when you wrote all the code? His benchmark is on GitHub to try for yourself.

Nolan Lawson

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Why Is This Fingerprinting Script 'Creating Bioweapons'? — A crawl of sites to collect canvas fingerprinting examples (which you can see, visually, at fingerprint.garden) found an anti-analysis technique where JavaScript identifiers were named after… taboo topics, with a prompt hidden in invisible Unicode, all designed to make LLMs refuse to work on the code!

Veritas

💡 Canvas fingerprinting is a technique that uses quirks of how different clients render canvas elements, in order to distinguish browser environments.

IN BRIEF:

  • 😄 Bartosz shares a creative way to generate strings and run code without parentheses or quotes. Good old JavaScript fun!

  • 📊 GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report has TypeScript as the most used language on GitHub by contributors (with JS at third), and ~44% of merged TypeScript PRs showing AI involvement. Plus a lot more besides.

  • GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target by default in public repos from December 2, unless an event policy explicitly allows it, with brownouts on November 9 & 16.

  • Cloudflare Workers now supports the Temporal API natively behind a temporal compatibility flag. It'll be available by default from December 1.

RELEASES:

  • Node.js v27.0 (Alpha) and v26.13.0 (LTS) – Node 26 is now the 'Lithium' LTS line, and 27 is the first ever Node 'alpha'. Under Node's new release process, every line spends six months in alpha before going Current.

  • Vitest 5.1 – A new --since-last-run flag reruns only tests affected by your edits, plus there's an interactive snapshot review feature.

  • Rspack 2.3 – The Rust-based webpack alternative adopts SWC Next and its rewritten parser. The team reports 5-20% faster builds and less peak memory use.

  • Leaflet 2.0 Beta 1 – The mapping library's first major in a decade goes tree-shakeable, ships TypeScript types, and drops its default export.

  • Effect 4.1, pnpm 12.17, ESLint 10.14.0, Nuxt DevTools v4

📖  Articles and Videos

"No, npm, 'estee' is not a typo of 'testem'" — Shane tried to publish a CLI called estee and hit npm's typosquatting filter, which (as best as we can tell) rejects names within a small Levenshtein distance of popular packages' names.

Shane Friedman

Shrinking clarity.js: When Cleaner Code Gzips Worse — Microsoft let an agent run 50+ size experiments on its analytics script. A big win came from dropping import * namespace objects, while good-practice refactors like extracting helpers actually made the gzipped output bigger.

Manu Nair (Microsoft)

Workshop: How to Implement Session Replay — Filters, custom tags, and sampling settings for finding the sessions that matter. Nov 5, 10am PT.

Sentry sponsor

'Nothing Installs at Our Company Until It's a Week Old' — Many recent package hijacks were caught within hours, so Bruno's company now makes new releases wait a week. He explains what this approach broke, what cooldowns don't stop, and settings for popular package managers.

Bruno Jurković

Timing Ten Design Systems, Then Fixing the Slow Ones — Den timed ten design systems (MUI, Ant Design, and Ionic among them) opening a 249-option select and ticking 100 checkboxes, then profiled the slow ones to find out why.

Den Odell

Using Bun? Dependabot Can't See Most of Your Dependencies — GitHub's dependency graph doesn't parse bun.lock, so Dependabot alerts cover only direct dependencies. Nicolas has some tips for improving matters.

Nicolas Charpentier (Shortcut)

📄 How Hard Is It to Check for Whitespace? – Why Java, Python and JavaScript disagree on what counts as whitespace. Sergey Tselovalnikov

📄 A Proposal: How to Hire Junior Engineers in the Age of AI – The npm co-founder thinks traditional coding interviews are dead. Laurie Voss

📄 How to Make postMessage Type-Safe in Under 350 Bytes Pavel Grinchenko (Evil Martians)

📄 The Web Can't Afford a JavaScript Runtime Monoculture Kate Holterhoff (RedMonk)

🛠 Code & Tools

Handwired: Compile Regular JavaScript into a Neural Net — A new mind-bender from Pretext's creator: a compiler that turns JavaScript into an exact network of ReLUs and matrix multiplies that run on the GPU. Demos include a 130-layer 'mini desktop' and a WebGPU search over 100K JSON documents.

Cheng Lou

Build Smarter JavaScript Applications With Live Search Data — Add search, shopping, maps, news, trends, flights and hotels results with a single developer-friendly JavaScript SDK.

SerpApi sponsor

🌐 x18n: Lint and Maintain i18n Files for Any Framework — Anthony Fu's successor to i18n-ally scans locale files and translation calls and reports missing, unused and broken keys (like how tsc --noEmit reports type errors).

Anthony Fu

djs: A New 'Suspend Anywhere' JavaScript Engine — Armin (of Flask fame) built an engine to run scripts in WebAssembly that can snapshot the VM's state and resume elsewhere, even mid-await.

Armin Ronacher

webframe: Run a Web Page Like a Command-Line Program — Point it at a URL or HTML file and it runs the page in a hidden system web view, piping console.log() to stdout and exceptions to stderr. No bundled browser or Playwright needed.

Jeff Lindsay

phoria2: A Small WebGL 2 Library for 3D Charts — A dependency-free 3D library aimed at dashboards and product viewers, with an API you can 'learn in an afternoon'. Plenty of live demos on the page.

Kevin Roast

  • Shiki 4.6 – Powerful code syntax highlighter, now with faster decoration handling and compressed Oniguruma WASM binary.

  • Preact 11.1 – A new preact/compat/compiler-runtime entry point lets code compiled by React Compiler run on Preact too.

  • Postgres.js 4.0 – The popular Postgres client for Node, Bun and Cloudflare Workers gets a rewrite and goes ESM-only.

Your coding agent can write the app. Expo is the agentic mobile infrastructure that takes it from a repo to the App Store.

  • ☕ CheerpJ 5.0 brings Java 21 and 25 to the browser via WebAssembly, ships the full JDK so you can compile Java in a tab, and previews a new WasmGC-based engine the team hopes will run Minecraft and IntelliJ one day.

  • 🤖 LLM-whisperer Simon Willison looks at the world of browser games being built with coding agents, and argues October was the point where agents got good enough to ship playable games.

  • 🕹️ Talking of games… GitHub's game jam Game Off is back for its 14th year with the theme 'SHIFT'. Entries are due on itch.io by December 1.

item.title: [Stefan Judis Web Development] Blake Watson on the state of the industry (#note)
item.description:
Here's Blake sharing his feelings about AI, software development and where we're all heading. He wrote the article that's been on my TODO list for a while. Let me comment on some highlights.

I feel like I will be able to build things I never have been able to before, but at the same time, I have heightened fears about being replaceable or less valuable in my job. If all I’m doing is prompting an AI bot, why am I being paid so much?

100% this. I'm scared and worried that the skills I put so much time into building are worth nothing. I used to be proud of my deep platform knowledge. Turns out Claude knows more.

And on a bigger scale, "personal software" is really happening. My friends are building browser extensions and websites for their fantasy football leagues. They don't care about quality as long as it gets the job done. Occasionally they ask me things about the DOOM (DOM), which is funny and scary at the same time.

At what point does software still need someone who actually knows what they're doing? I guess we'll find out soon enough.

If you haven’t used one of these coding tools in the last six months, you probably don’t have a good idea of what they are capable of.

I admire people who are still holding out against this technology, I really do. If that's you, you rock! Unfortunately, I couldn't agree more with the statement above.

If your arguments about LLM quality and all the generated fake news (hallucinations) are based on Copilot tryouts around last Christmas, you'd better check again. Things have changed a lot.

I just have this icky feeling when I use it.

Same. I hate that I can create things without effort or understanding. I hate that there are days when I talk to agents all day. I hate that it seems like nothing matters anymore. I hate that everyone is pushing and pushing and pushing and nothing gets done.

I’m worried about being replaced, but maybe I’ll be even more valuable. [...] So I just go back and forth. I worry about it, but then I think everything will work out.

Yes. There are good weeks and then there are bad weeks.

Sometimes, I'm okay with "focusing on the outcome". Sometimes, I'm fine with the loss of the job that was my favorite thing to do. Sometimes, I have enough energy to change habits and find satisfaction and joy elsewhere.

But sometimes, man... sometimes the new world drives me nuts.

So, let's hope Blake is right and things will work out (somehow).

item.title: [Stefan Judis Web Development] Web Weekly #201 (#blogPost)
item.description:
Guten Tag! Guten Tag! 👋

Do you know what happens when you import the same module multiple times? Do you think we need a new poster element? And have you ever used the vary header to improve caching?

Turn on the Web Weekly tune and find some answers below. Enjoy!

::: song by="Dom" title="Twenty One Pilots - Center Mass" youtube="PAbv0MXFYgE" I really like the shift from a hip-hop style to a full rock ending, and the lyrics are well written around the topic of vulnerability and loss. :::

Do you want to share your favorite song with the Web Weekly community? Hit reply; there are three more songs left in the queue.

I try to avoid bringing up my mood about "all the vibes" too much in this newsletter, but the change in the industry is the stickiest topic ever. And regardless of whether the industry collapses or not, I don't think the technology will disappear. Cheap open source models can do certain things better and faster than I can. They'll probably survive, like it or not.

So here are my two AI takes for today.

AI makes projects with weak engineering culture fail much faster.

Florian describes the scenario of teams that are just shipping. They move fast but lose control quickly. I see that around me and it shows the real challenge if you're using AI for coding. It's just too easy to cover a lot of ground. Taking on the responsibility of understanding what's going on while establishing good practices and judgment will be one of the most important skills going forward. My brain wants all the shortcuts, and yours probably does too. Not taking them is the real challenge.

You need to find some way to leverage your expertise to do what the models can’t.

I was hesitant for a long time, but frankly I became too scared to ignore what's going on because it's still a long time until I'm ready for retirement.

That's why I follow what's happening closely and try things myself to know what's hype and what's real. It's obvious that the machines are pretty good at certain tasks. Busy work is one of them. But there are still areas they're "not great" at.

It's important to understand the technology's weak spots. I watch out for areas to apply my strengths. As Sean puts it, there will be areas in which you'll be better than the machines.

This topic is heated and emotional, so I just wanted to share where I'm at right now. I also guess there are many Web Weekly readers that aren't thrilled about the new world. If that's you, hang in there! And if you want to share your thoughts with me, you can always hit reply.

If you enjoy Web Weekly, share it with your friends and family.

  • 🦋 Bluesky
  • 🐘 Mastodon
  • 💼 LinkedIn

A quick "repost" really helps this indie newsletter out. Thank you! ❤️

Web Weekly Housekeeping

Last week, I shared the new Connection-Allowlist header and Nicolas told me that the implementation has already started in Firefox. 🎉

And because I mentioned complicated CSP configuration, Mark shared with me how the strict-dynamic directive can help tame all this CSP madness.

And of course, as always, I want to give a huge shoutout to the 58 Web Weekly supporters!

Thank you so much for supporting Web Weekly. Your small gestures really keep me going in the time of the slopocalypse. If you also want to support indie publishing, you can do so on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

Something that made me smile this week

Nothing spectacular: it's just Frank who drew his own emoji collection one by one. You can get it on frankmoji.com.

Express yourself

No code

  • Don't be nice → "If you hear enough people say something it somehow becomes 'just another opinion.'"
  • how to find meaning in ordinary days → "not all loneliness needs to be cured. some of it just needs to be sat with."
  • You should never be angry at work → "Angry engineers are rarely the ones holding the company together, but they’re also rarely useless."

The example.com redesign

So, example.com got a redesign. 👆 People asked why and the VP of IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) replied that it was to save bandwidth. The new site now enriches the page with a single s.js file so that bots, curls, or whatever can save some bytes. Wild!

Load less

Responsive iframes

Who would have thought that I'd plug an iframe change that I'm actually excited about? I had to deal with resizing iframes quite a bit, so this platform addition is more than welcome. So if you're updating iframe sizes manually, you'll dig this!

Be aware that responsive iframes are cutting-edge and Chromium-only so far.

Automatically resize

AI policies

You might have heard that Sindre, who maintains a gazillion open source projects in the JS ecosystem, closed external contributions. This means you can't simply contribute to his projects anymore.

Of course, I'm not maintaining that many or that successful projects, but I see myself making more and more things private on GitHub. I just can't be bothered anymore.

On top of that, I also receive five emails per week from "fake Web Weekly readers" who want to plug their posts and projects. The bold ones even include a personal agent signature. The new world is just wasting everyone's time.

Regardless, before closing everything, maybe adding an AI policy is worth a shot.

Define some rules

Kinda related side note: do you know that GitHub now highlights your projects' accessibility statements? 👏

Do we need a <poster> element?

Scott thinks so and is yet again on the journey of extending the web. Scott was also part of bringing lazy loading to videos, and he's on to the next topic: responsive images in video elements.

I love these stories.

Control the preview

The wonderful weird web – The restroom archive

The Restroom Archive is an ongoing repository of publicly accessible restrooms. [...] Currently, 40 archivists have documented 193 restrooms in 85 cities across 13 countries.

What? I have no words. 😅 And before you wonder, the site lists 3D models of restrooms. I checked seven restrooms and they were reasonably clean.

Take a break

The tricky vary header

Cloudflare added support for the vary header. It's fair if you now think "Alright, why would I care?". The post does a good job explaining what vary does and why caching is hard (obviously).

Control the cache

Import, import, and import

What happens when you call import('foo.js') twice? Joan explains how the module map works and that there will be only one network call. But what if the first import fails and you want to try again? That used to be tricky, but turns out, there's a spec change rolling out as we speak.

Overfetch

Modern Web Types

If you're using cutting-edge web features, you probably run into the situation that TypeScript doesn't know about new properties yet because it only includes types for features supported by two engines (TIL!). Philip was so annoyed by this that he released modern-web-types which includes features that are only supported by one engine.

But, as mentioned in the post, you shouldn't rely on TypeScript for feature detection or support info. That's where proper Baseline tooling comes in.

Ride the cutting edge

Some interop "things"

I think the submission of Interop focus areas for next year is closed by now, but you can still chime in and add your thumb to your favorites on GitHub.

The fine folks at Firefox also built a nice UI to rank your most preferred new web features. The data goes to the Firefox team as far as I understand.

And the web dev community is still around (❤️) and blogged about their favorite features, too.

  • My Interop 2027 picks from Paweł
  • My Interop 2027 Rankings from Declan
  • My top picks for Interop 2027 from Sara

And if you want to dive into this rabbit hole, the community links back and forth between all these posts. Love ya!

Random MDN – ::details-content

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

Just a quick reminder: ::details-content is a thing these days.

Style the content

New on the baseline

The alpha() CSS function became Baseline newly available and Object.groupBy() is now widely available.

Three valuable projects to have a look at

  • zachleat/table-of-contents – A table of contents web component.
  • Homebrew/BrewUI – Homebrew's official macOS GUI.
  • Wox-launcher/Wox – A cross-platform launcher.

A new Tiny Helper

If you're looking for a quick way to create mockups with phones on a nice background, Sliick indeed looks slicker than many other tools that do that.

Do a photo shoot

Find more single-purpose online tools on tiny-helpers.dev.

Thought of the week

Here's Sean on playing company politics...

If you have powerful enemies at a company (for instance, the CTO or an influential VP doesn’t like you), quit.

Did you learn something from this issue?

❤️ If so, join 58 other Web Weekly supporters and give back with a small monthly donation on Patreon or GitHub Sponsors.

This is all, friends!

Loved this email? Hated this email? I want to hear about it!

If you think something needs improvement or something sparked some joy, reply to this email because I want to know more!

And with that, take care of yourself - mentally, physically, and emotionally.

I'll see you next week! 👋

Reply to Stefan
